abstract: Many animals and plants have evolved to rely on microbiome mediated interactions with their environment. Across diverse insect groups, many are incapable of either breaking down complex carbohydrates or synthesizing essential nutrients despite consuming diets which should require one, or both, functions. Onthophagus beetles are one such host, with recent work suggesting their ability to digest their dung diet, typically rich in tough to digest polysaccharides and poor in nutrients, is likely bolstered by heritable symbionts. Despite there being over 2,000 species of Onthophagus, and over 5,000 species of "true" dung beetles (Scarabaeinae), little is known about how the microbiomes of these beetles modulate their interactions with their dung diet. The work presented here assesses the possible significance of four individual microbiome members, present during Onthophagus taurus development. Results show that three of the four isolates tested partially recovered normative developmental outcomes in O. taurus. Specifically, inoculation with a strain of either Acinetobacter, Brucella, or Pseudomonas increased pupal size relative to beetles deprived of the maternal inoculate. This mirrors the effects of individuals receiving the full natural inoculate, which contains hundreds of bacterial species. Further, using whole genome sequencing, we form a hypothesis of what nutrients these isolates provide to benefit O. taurus development. The findings presented here further highlight Onthophagus dung beetles as powerful systems to study the complex ways in which microbiome function can interact with diet to influence developmental and evolutionary outcomes.
